tier_reason: First-party hyperfine tables in the README with public commands (justfile bench and bench-stream recipes) and a named machine (MacBook M3 Pro), but the rustc version is not stated and the baseline sort, uniq and awk binaries have no stated implementation, version or build flags, so it falls short of A; no independent measurement.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README table (MacBook M3 Pro, hyperfine): hist 231.5 ms vs naive 'sort | uniq -c | sort -n' 5637.6 ms (Relative column 24.35x; repo description says 25x), naive with -S 1G 5610.1 ms (24.23x), LC_ALL=C 1219.5 ms (5.27x), LC_ALL=C plus -S 1G 1179.2 ms (5.09x), awk count pipeline 1265.4 ms (5.47x), uutils coreutils pipeline with --parallel 1 890.1 ms (3.84x); other Rust tools cuniq 2.43x, huniq 12.16x, sortuniq 13.68x. Dedup mode: hist -u 180.6 ms vs awk '!seen[$0]++' 1307.1 ms (7.24x), ripuniq 1.19x, huniq 12.95x. All ratios are printed in the page's Relative column.
corrections.workload: justfile: nucgen -n 1000000 -l 20 writes 1M FASTQ records, i.e. 4M lines: 1M unique '@seq.N' headers, 1M random 20-nt sequences (effectively all unique), 1M identical '+' lines and 1M identical 20-character '?' quality lines (nucgen src/main.rs and src/write.rs), so about 2M distinct lines out of 4M. Each tool reads the file on stdin and writes to a file; hyperfine --warmup=10 --shell=bash. Second benchmark (bench-stream) prints first occurrences only (hist -u).
corrections.baseline: Plain 'sort | uniq -c | sort -n' as found on PATH (the README calls it coreutils; on macOS the default sort and uniq are the BSD-derived system tools unless GNU coreutils shadows them; implementation and versions not stated), in the default locale and with LC_ALL=C; also uutils coreutils sort/uniq with --parallel 1 and an awk pipeline (awk implementation not stated; README links the gawk manual).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: hist: Cargo.toml [profile.release] lto = true, codegen-units = 1, debug = false (default opt-level 3); .cargo/config.toml rustflags -C target-cpu=native; edition 2024; rustc version not stated. Baselines are prebuilt system or installed binaries with unknown versions and build flags.
corrections.caveats: Most of the headline 24x comes from locale-aware collation in the default-locale sort: with LC_ALL=C the gap is 5.27x and against uutils sort (single-threaded) 3.84x. The input is not 'almost all unique': half of its 4M lines are two values repeated 1M times each, the other half are unique, so the hash table holds about 2M keys. The speedup is algorithmic (hash counting with hashbrown over a bumpalo arena, then sorting only the distinct entries) against a three-process pipe that sorts every line; it is not a language-level effect. Outputs are not byte-identical: hist writes 'count<TAB>line' through a csv writer (lines containing tabs or quotes get quoted, non-UTF-8 lines error), ties come out in unstable order, and the awk row sorts descending. First-party, one machine, no baseline versions. No LICENSE file in the repo: MIT is declared only in Cargo.toml and on crates.io (0.1.8), and the README badge links a LICENSE.md that returns 404. Sibling tools huniq and cuniq are already listed separately in wave 14.
corrections.why_faster: From src/main.rs: one pass over stdin with bstr for_byte_line, counting in a hashbrown HashMap via the raw_entry API with keys copied once into a bumpalo arena, then sort_unstable of only the distinct (line, count) pairs; the baseline pipe sorts all 4M lines (with locale collation by default), runs uniq over the sorted stream, then sorts again. Algorithmic, not language-level.

notes: Numbers match the README exactly (the ratios are on the page, not derived). Main shortcomings for the record: the 24x is mostly the default-locale sort (5.3x with LC_ALL=C, 3.8x vs uutils), the workload is a FASTQ file in which half the lines are two repeated values, baseline tool implementations and versions are unstated, and the licence is declared only in Cargo.toml (no LICENSE file).

tier_reason: First-party README table against PyMuPDF (MuPDF) and pypdfium2 (PDFium) with no hardware, compiler, library versions or published harness for the table's 60 s-timeout/p99 run; scripts/bench_pymupdf.py covers only the PyMuPDF side, so not A, and nothing independent was found for B.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the README table. Cargo.toml [profile.release]: opt-level 3, lto = true, codegen-units = 1; rustc version not stated. Baseline versions not stated (scripts/benchmark_requirements.txt only sets minimums: pymupdf>=1.28.2, pypdfium2>=5.13.0).
corrections.caveats: Hardware, compiler, library versions and the harness behind the README table are not published: scripts/bench_pymupdf.py times PyMuPDF open plus a Python per-page get_text loop with time.perf_counter over the same three corpora (trying up to 9 passwords on encrypted files and skipping bomb files), but no matching pypdfium2 or PDFOxide runner with the stated 60 s timeout and p99 was found. The CHANGELOG (0.3.5) says the PDFOxide corpus numbers come from a Rust verify_corpus example binary, which is no longer at examples/verify_corpus.rs. The PDFOxide row is identical (0.8 ms, p99 9 ms) in the 'Python Libraries' and 'Rust Libraries' tables, so it may be a native Rust measurement compared against Python-wrapped C and C++ engines; that it went through the Python binding is not established. 2,907 of the 3,830 PDFs are small veraPDF compliance fixtures, so the mean per document mostly measures fixed per-file overhead; lopdf (parse only, no extraction) shows 0.3 ms. Pass rate and output differ by tool (scripts/bench_compare.py counts a file as 'clean' even when only PDFOxide's character set is a superset of PyMuPDF's), so equal work is not shown. CHANGELOG 0.3.5 reported p50 0.6 ms and p99 33 ms on the same corpus, and the README does not say which version was measured. MuPDF and PDFium are already listed (wave 10). First-party claim from a project whose stated motive is replacing PyMuPDF.
corrections.workload: Text extraction from 3,830 PDFs (veraPDF 2,907, Mozilla pdf.js 897, DARPA SafeDocs 26), single thread, 60 s timeout, no warm-up, mean and p99 time per document; text-only libraries, no OCR (README Performance section).
corrections.why_faster: Not stated in the README. Not attributable to the language: different extraction pipelines, and the baselines' timings include the Python per-page call overhead of their bindings, while the PDFOxide figure may come from the native Rust runner.

notes: README numbers match the record (0.8 ms vs 4.6 ms and 4.1 ms; ratios 5.8x and 5.1x derived from page data). Main shortcomings for the record: no hardware, versions or published harness for the table, the PDFOxide row may be native Rust against Python-wrapped baselines, and the corpus is dominated by tiny conformance fixtures. pdf.oxide.fyi/docs/performance (the full-methodology page) did not resolve (ENOTFOUND).

tier_reason: First-party README and PERFORMANCE_ANALYSIS.md table against system grep with no published grep command, pattern, grep version, CPU model or run count; the repo's Criterion benches measure only xerg's internal file readers, not grep.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README and PERFORMANCE_ANALYSIS.md ('Final Performance Validation', 2025-11-13): large dataset (target/ directory) system grep 28,122 ms vs xerg 1,590 ms (17.7x) and xerg -x 835 ms (33.7x); single file (src/main.rs) 4.0 ms vs 3.0 ms (README: 25% speedup; PERFORMANCE_ANALYSIS: 1.33x); src/ set of about 8 files 3.0 ms vs 3.0 ms (parity) and -x 4.0 ms (slower). The README's mode table contradicts the main table (default '23x', CPU 650% and 690%).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: 'Release builds' (README); Cargo.toml has no [profile.release] section, so default cargo release settings (opt-level 3, no LTO); rustc version not stated; grep version and flags not stated.
corrections.hardware: 'macOS, Multi-core system' (README); 'MacBook with full-power mode enabled' (PERFORMANCE_ANALYSIS.md); CPU model not stated
corrections.workload: Search one pattern (not stated) over a Rust target/ build directory, over src/main.rs, and over src/ (about 8 files) with system grep and with xerg; timings at 1 ms resolution; the grep command line and number of runs are not published.
corrections.caveats: The work differs from grep's: in multi-file mode xerg reads each file with BufReader::lines() and silently skips every line that is not valid UTF-8 without running the regex on it (src/search/xtreme.rs and default.rs), so the binary artefacts that fill a target/ directory are largely not searched, while grep scans every byte; the crawler (walkdir) also skips hidden files and directories such as the .fingerprint directories under target/debug and target/release. On top of that the win is parallelism (rayon scope; 484% to 745% CPU vs about 96% for grep). Pattern, grep implementation and version (probably BSD grep on macOS), CPU model and run count are not stated, the README's two tables disagree (17.7x vs '23x'), and there is no comparison with ripgrep (listed in wave 11), which does the same parallel work. The README's 'PCRE support' claim is wrong: it uses the Rust regex crate. Tiny learning project from a bootcamp (3 stars, 142 crates.io downloads). The speed-up is not attributable to the language.
corrections.why_faster: Parallel per-file scanning on a rayon scope plus less work: lines that are not valid UTF-8 are skipped without matching and hidden directories are not walked (src/search/xtreme.rs, default.rs, crawler.rs). Not language-level.

notes: Numbers match the README and PERFORMANCE_ANALYSIS.md. Main shortcomings for the record: unequal work (non-UTF-8 lines and hidden directories skipped, so binary build output is mostly not searched), parallel vs single-threaded grep, no published grep command, pattern, version or CPU, and internally inconsistent README tables; it could fall to D if an enricher shows the target/ comparison is dominated by skipped binary content.
